sections.title: Smoothness from a Lipschitz gradient: Smooth.lean
sections.intro: This file proves the quadratic upper model from differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient. Its proof studies a scalar function on the segment from $x$ to $y$, proves that its derivative is nonpositive, and compares its endpoint values. No Hessian or line-integral hypothesis is introduced.

blocks.title: Ambient space and namespace
blocks.explanation:
The scoped opening enables notation for nonnegative real numbers. The namespace prefixes each exported theorem with \lean{GradientDescent}. The typeclass variables describe a complete real inner-product space $H$. Completeness is needed here for Mathlib's gradient, the Riesz representative of the Fr\'echet derivative:
\[Df(x)[v]=\ip{\nabla f(x)}{v}.\]

blocks.title: The precise smoothness goal
blocks.explanation:
The hypotheses supply differentiability at every point and a globally $L$-Lipschitz gradient. The type of $L$ already includes $L\ge0$; its coercion is used in real arithmetic. Neither strong convexity nor a positive step size is required. The proof must establish, for arbitrary $x,y\in H$,
\[f(y)\le f(x)+\ip{\nabla f(x)}{y-x}+\frac L2\norm{y-x}^{2}.\]
The keyword \lean{by} begins the tactic proof of this inequality.

blocks.title: Define the corrected segment restriction
blocks.explanation:
The four \lean{let} declarations introduce local definitions, not new assumptions. Write $d=y-x$, $a=\ip{\nabla f(x)}{d}$, and $b=\norm d^2$. The scalar function is
\[q(t)=f(x+td)-f(x)-ta-\frac L2t^2b.\]
Subtracting the affine model and the quadratic correction makes the desired result equivalent to $q(1)\le q(0)=0$. Later \lean{dsimp} can unfold these definitions.

blocks.title: Differentiate the affine path
blocks.explanation:
The parameterized \lean{have hline} proves a derivative statement for every real $t$. Start with the identity derivative $1$, multiply by the fixed vector $d$ using \lean{smul_const}, and add the constant vector $x$ using \lean{const_add}. This gives
\[\frac{d}{ds}(x+sd)\big|_{s=t}=1\mathbin{\cdot}d=d.\]
The final \lean{simpa using} simplifies the derivative vector $1\mathbin{\cdot}d$ and transfers the chained proof to the displayed goal.

blocks.title: Apply the chain rule and identify the gradient
blocks.explanation:
At $x+td$, \lean{hf} gives differentiability and \lean{hasFDerivAt} supplies its Fr\'echet derivative. The method \lean{comp_hasDerivAt} composes that derivative with \lean{hline t}. Its resulting scalar derivative is $Df(x+td)[d]$. The simplifier unfolds function composition and rewrites the gradient inner product in the goal to $Df(x+td)[d]$ using \lean{inner_gradient_left}, so the goal matches the chain-rule proof. This establishes
\[\frac{d}{ds}f(x+sd)\big|_{s=t}=\ip{\nabla f(x+td)}{d}.\]
This is the reusable local fact \lean{hcomp t}.

blocks.title: Build a derivative proof for q
blocks.explanation:
The chained derivative lemmas differentiate the expression defining $q$: \lean{sub_const} subtracts $f(x)$; the first \lean{sub} subtracts $ta$; and the second subtracts $(L/2)t^2b$. The identity derivative followed by \lean{pow 2}, \lean{const_mul}, and \lean{mul_const} proves the quadratic term's derivative. The pipe \lean{|>} passes that proof to the following method call. The claimed simplified derivative is
\[q'(t)=\ip{\nabla f(x+td)}{d}-a-Ltb.\]
The tactic \lean{convert ... using 1} uses the constructed derivative proof while leaving equality obligations for its function and derivative expressions.

blocks.title: Resolve the two conversion equalities
blocks.explanation:
The first bullet resolves equality of functions. The tactic \lean{ext s} applies function extensionality, reducing it to equality at an arbitrary argument $s$. The listed simplifications unfold $q$, pointwise function subtraction and powers, and the identity function. The second bullet resolves equality of derivative values. After simplifying the identity function, \lean{ring} checks the polynomial identity
\[\frac L2(2t)b=Ltb.\]
Thus \lean{hq} is an actual derivative proof, not merely a proposed formula.

blocks.title: Set up the nonpositive-derivative goal
blocks.explanation:
The next local lemma takes $t$ in the interior of $[0,1]$ and aims to prove
\[\ip{
abla f(x+td)}{d}-a-Ltb\le0.\]
The library fact \lean{interior_subset} places $t$ in the closed interval. Membership there is a pair of inequalities; projecting its first component with \lean{.1} gives $0\le t$. This sign is essential when simplifying $
orm{td}=|t|
orm d$ to $t
orm d$.

blocks.title: Apply gradient Lipschitzness along the segment
blocks.explanation:
The method \lean{hLip.dist_le_mul} applies the global Lipschitz bound at $x+td$ and $x$. The simplifier converts distances to norms, simplifies $(x+td)-x$, expands the norm of a scalar multiple, and removes $|t|$ using $t\ge0$. Associativity puts the product into the desired form:
\[
orm{
abla f(x+td)-
abla f(x)}\le Lt
orm d.\]
No sign of an inner product is assumed in this step.

blocks.title: Cauchy--Schwarz proves the derivative sign
blocks.explanation:
The fact \lean{hinner} is the signed Cauchy--Schwarz bound, and \lean{hprod} multiplies the Lipschitz bound by $
orm d\ge0$. Rewriting with \lean{inner_sub_left} expands the gradient difference in the first inner-product argument. The tactic \lean{dsimp} unfolds $a,b$ in the goal. The two bounds then read
\[\ip{
abla f(x+td)}{d}-a
 \le
orm{
abla f(x+td)-
abla f(x)}
orm d
 \le Lt
orm d^2=Ltb.\]
The tactic \lean{nlinarith} combines these real inequalities and moves $Ltb$ to the left.

blocks.title: Prove antitonicity through three obligations
blocks.explanation:
Applying \lean{antitoneOn_of_deriv_nonpos} to the convex interval $[0,1]$ leaves three goals, discharged by the three bullets:
\begin{itemize}
\item Continuity on the closed interval: each \lean{hq t} implies continuity at $t$; the equivalence for pointwise continuity gives global continuity, which is restricted using \lean{continuousOn}.
\item Differentiability on its interior: each \lean{hq t} gives differentiability at $t$; the explicitly typed \lean{show} assembles a global differentiability proof, then restricts it.
\item Nonpositive derivative at each interior point: \lean{intro} introduces $t$ and its membership proof, \lean{rw [(hq t).deriv]} replaces the actual derivative by the proved formula, and \lean{hq_nonpos} supplies its sign.
\end{itemize}
The resulting \lean{AntitoneOn} statement means $s\le t$ implies $q(t)\le q(s)$ for $s,t\in[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Evaluate the decreasing function at zero and one
blocks.explanation:
Applying \lean{hanti} to $0\le1$ gives $q(1)\le q(0)$. The inline \lean{by simp} proofs certify endpoint membership, while \lean{norm_num} certifies the numerical order. Unfolding the four local definitions and simplifying scalar multiplication, powers, and zero terms gives
\[f\bigl(x+(y-x)\bigr)-f(x)-\ip{\nabla f(x)}{y-x}
       -\frac L2\norm{y-x}^2\le0.\]
The side proof $2\ne0$ is passed to the simplification rule for $0^2$.

blocks.title: Finish by additive algebra and rearrangement
blocks.explanation:
The tactic \lean{abel} proves $x+(y-x)=y$ using only the additive commutative-group laws. The rewrite replaces the endpoint in \lean{hfinal}. The remaining inequality is linear in the displayed real expressions:
\[f(y)-f(x)-\ip{\nabla f(x)}{y-x}-\frac L2\norm{y-x}^2\le0.\]
The tactic \lean{linarith} rearranges this into the theorem's upper-bound goal. The proof is now complete.

sections.title: Auxiliary Euler-step estimates: Step.lean
sections.intro: These estimates are deliberately stated for arbitrary vector values $g_x,g_y$, or for an arbitrary map $g$. Their inputs are strong monotonicity and Lipschitzness, rather than calculus. They are later applied to the gradient with a small auxiliary step to construct a minimizer. The contraction condition here does not replace the convergence theorem's full condition $0<\alpha<2/L$.

blocks.title: An inner-product space is enough for the estimates
blocks.explanation:
The namespace and scoped notation are the same as in the smoothness file. These variables assume a real inner-product space, but do not assume completeness: norm expansions and the Lipschitz estimate need no limit argument. A later application of Banach's theorem adds completeness. The underlying identities are
\[
orm{u-v}^{2}=
orm u^2-2\ip{u}{v}+
orm v^2,
 \qquad 
orm{hu}=|h|
orm u.\]

blocks.title: State the squared-step estimate for arbitrary values
blocks.explanation:
The vectors \lean{gx} and \lean{gy} stand for $g_x,g_y$; there is no function or gradient assumption hidden in the statement. The supplied inequalities are strong monotonicity and a Lipschitz bound at the selected pair. For $h\ge0$ the goal is
\[\norm{(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)}^2
 \le (1-2hm+h^2L^2)\norm{x-y}^2.\]
The constant $m$ need not be positive for this elementary lemma. The sign $h\ge0$ controls the scaling of its monotonicity input.

blocks.title: Square the Lipschitz inequality legally
blocks.explanation:
Let $A=\norm{g_x-g_y}$ and $D=\norm{x-y}$. The assumption is $A\le LD$, and all three numbers $A,D,L$ are nonnegative. Therefore
\[A^2\le L^2D^2.\]
The tactic \lean{nlinarith} proves this polynomial consequence using the explicit norm-nonnegativity facts and the nonnegativity built into $L$. Supplying those facts makes the squaring step valid; an arbitrary signed inequality could not simply be squared.

blocks.title: Scale the two bounds with nonnegative factors
blocks.explanation:
The lemma \lean{mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left} preserves an inequality when multiplied by a nonnegative number. The tactic \lean{positivity} proves $0\le2h$ from $h\ge0$, and \lean{sq_nonneg h} proves $0\le h^2$. With $d=x-y$ and $v=g_x-g_y$, the saved inequalities are
\[2hm\norm d^2\le2h\ip{v}{d},\qquad
 h^2\norm v^2\le h^2L^2\norm d^2.\]
The first will be subtracted, and the second added, in the norm expansion.

blocks.title: Expand the squared norm and combine the inequalities
blocks.explanation:
Inside \lean{rw}, the embedded \lean{show ... by module} proves the vector identity $(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)=d-hv$ by module algebra. The listed rewrites expand its squared norm, pull $h$ out of the inner product and norm, replace the real norm by absolute value, use $|h|=h$, and swap inner-product arguments. The goal becomes the real inequality
\[\norm d^2-2h\ip{v}{d}+h^2\norm v^2
       \le(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\norm d^2.\]
Subtracting the first scaled bound and adding the second proves it; \lean{nlinarith} carries out exactly that polynomial combination.

blocks.title: State the corresponding norm bound
blocks.explanation:
This theorem has the same pairwise assumptions and aims to remove the square:
\[\norm{(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)}
       \le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\,\norm{x-y}.\]
Here and below the square root has Mathlib's total real convention: it is zero on negative inputs. A separate hypothesis that the coefficient is nonnegative is therefore unnecessary; the squared-step bound already rules out a negative right-hand side when the relevant distance is nonzero.

blocks.title: Take the square root and simplify its product
blocks.explanation:
The local \lean{hsq} applies the preceding theorem. Writing $Q=1-2hm+h^2L^2$ and $D=\norm{x-y}$, \lean{Real.le_sqrt_of_sq_le} turns its conclusion into
\[\norm{(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)}\le\sqrt{QD^2}.\]
The rewrite \lean{Real.sqrt_mul'} factors this as $\sqrt Q\sqrt{D^2}$ because $D^2\ge0$; \lean{Real.sqrt_sq} then uses $D\ge0$ to give $\sqrt{D^2}=D$. The tactic \lean{rwa ... at hbound} both performs these rewrites in the saved inequality and uses it to close the goal.

blocks.title: Package a globally contracting step
blocks.explanation:
Now the input is an actual map $g:H\to H$. Strong monotonicity holds at every pair, and \lean{LipschitzWith L g} supplies the global Lipschitz bound. The conditions are $\alpha>0$ and $\alpha L^2<2m$. Define
\[T(x)=x-\alpha g(x),\quad Q=1-2\alpha m+\alpha^2L^2,
       \quad q=\sqrt Q.\]
The pair notation packages $q$ as a nonnegative real, with \lean{Real.sqrt_nonneg} proving its sign. The conclusion \lean{ContractingWith} requires both $q<1$ and that $T$ is $q$-Lipschitz.

blocks.title: Split contraction and show its squared coefficient is below one
blocks.explanation:
The tactic \lean{constructor} splits the contraction conclusion into its two components. The first bullet concerns $q<1$; \lean{change} displays it as a real square-root inequality by unfolding the nonnegative-real packaging. The hypothesis \lean{hsmall} gives $2m-\alpha L^2>0$, and \lean{mul_pos} multiplies it by $\alpha>0$. Thus
\[1-Q=\alpha(2m-\alpha L^2)>0,\qquad Q<1.\]
The tactic \lean{nlinarith} expands this product and establishes the saved fact \lean{hq}.

blocks.title: Turn Q below one into a square-root contraction factor
blocks.explanation:
Since the comparison value $1$ is positive, the library equivalence \lean{Real.sqrt_lt_sqrt_iff_of_pos} turns $Q<1$ into $\sqrt Q<\sqrt1$. Its projection \lean{.2} selects the implication from the ordinary inequality to the square-root inequality. The proof \lean{by norm_num} certifies $0<1$, and \lean{simpa only [Real.sqrt_one]} simplifies the result to
\[q=\sqrt Q<1.\]
This equivalence also handles $Q<0$ under the total square-root convention.

blocks.title: Reduce the second component to a distance estimate
blocks.explanation:
The second main bullet proves that $T$ is $q$-Lipschitz. Applying \lean{LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul} reduces it to an inequality at arbitrary points, introduced by \lean{intro x y}. Applying the original Lipschitz hypothesis at that pair and rewriting distances as norms produces the saved input
\[\norm{g(x)-g(y)}\le L\norm{x-y}.\]
This is the pairwise Lipschitz assumption needed by \lean{gradient_step_contract}.

blocks.title: Apply the norm estimate and complete the contraction proof
blocks.explanation:
The simplifier changes the target distances into norms. The tactic \lean{change} exposes the coercion of $q$ and the definition of the step map, leaving
\[\norm{(x-\alpha g(x))-(y-\alpha g(y))}
       \le\sqrt Q\,\norm{x-y}.\]
The final \lean{exact} supplies the already-proved pairwise norm theorem with $g_x=g(x)$, $g_y=g(y)$, the nonnegative step obtained by the order projection \lean{.le}, strong monotonicity at $x,y$, and the saved bound \lean{hb}. Both contraction components are now proved.
